# Waydroid-box — feasibility assessment

Yes, your goal is technically achievable in principle, but there is an important distinction: you want to use your Linux Mint PC as the *display and input client*, while your Steam Deck OLED does all the Android computing.

Your intended architecture is:

PC client — Linux Mint

Display Android • Keyboard • Mouse

LAN connection — remote display and input

Steam Deck OLED — host

Waydroid • Android apps • CPU • GPU • RAM

Computing stays on the Deck

The important part is that SSH alone does not transfer Waydroid's graphical interface to your PC. SSH can launch and manage processes on the Deck, but you also need a suitable way to stream the Android display to Linux Mint and send keyboard, mouse and touch input back.

## The main technical obstacle

Waydroid is designed to run on a Linux system with a suitable graphics environment. Its normal graphical session integrates with the host's Wayland compositor and GPU. It isn't inherently a remote Android streaming service.

![]()

waydroid/docs · GitHub

\+1

So our project must solve two separate problems:

* Remote execution: launch and control Waydroid on SteamOS through your existing SSH connection.  
* Remote graphics: display the Deck-rendered Android interface on Linux Mint, with responsive mouse and keyboard input.

## Possible approaches

![How to connect to the screen of an android phone remotely with SCRCPY and SSH.][image1]

1\. Waydroid \+ remote display bridge

Run Waydroid on the Deck and investigate whether an Android display capture/streaming bridge can deliver its output to Linux Mint. This is the closest match to your goal, but compatibility and GPU behavior need testing.

![Sunshine Moonlight and Moondeck Buddy][image2]

2\. Remote desktop or game-streaming solution

Stream a Deck-hosted graphical session to the PC. This may be practical if Waydroid can run in that session, but it adds a graphical-session requirement and may be more complex than necessary.

Neither approach is confirmed to work on your Steam Deck OLED yet. We should verify the actual SteamOS kernel, graphics stack and session requirements before choosing one.

## Proposed waydroid-box acceptance criteria

| Requirement | Target |
| ----- | ----- |
| Android runtime | Steam Deck |
| CPU and RAM workload | Steam Deck |
| Android GPU rendering | Steam Deck, hardware acceleration if supported |
| Display and input | Linux Mint PC |
| Launch and stop | Manual commands through SSH |
| Network | Existing LAN |
| Startup at boot | Disabled |
| SteamOS modifications | Minimize; inspect requirements first |

One caveat: video encoding on the Deck and decoding on the PC will also consume resources. The PC will never be completely idle, but Android application processing and rendering should remain on the Deck if we choose the architecture correctly.

## My recommendation

Proceed with a read-only feasibility audit before creating or installing anything. The key question is whether Waydroid can run reliably on the SteamOS host and expose its graphical output to a remote client without requiring an unsupported host modification.

One question before we plan the first test:

What do you want to see on the Linux Mint PC?

Only the Android screen or app, in its own window

The entire Steam Deck desktop, including Waydroid

Should Waydroid run while the Deck is in desktop mode?

Yes — use the existing Steam Deck desktop session

No — prefer a dedicated session that doesn't require the Deck's desktop to be open

For the proposed waydroid-box project, display preference: Android screen/app in its own PC window; execution preference: use the existing Steam Deck desktop session. Continue with a read-only feasibility audit, no installation or modifications.

## Read-only audit: preliminary findings

The official documentation confirms three important facts:

1. Waydroid shares the host Linux kernel and uses Linux namespaces. It is a container-based Android environment, not a separate Android computer.  
2. ![]()  
3. waydroid/docs · GitHub  
4. \+1  
5. Waydroid's graphical session connects to a Wayland compositor. The documented startup sequence separates container startup from the user-level graphical session.  
6. ![]()  
7. GitHub  
8. \+1  
9. scrcpy is not automatically the answer. It is designed to mirror and control Android devices through Android Debug Bridge (ADB), but Waydroid is an Android container on the Deck, not a separate physical Android device. We'd need to verify whether its ADB interface and display capture support the workflow you want.  
10. ![]()  
11. GitHub  
12. \+1

The main unknown is therefore not whether the Deck can perform the computation. It is how to deliver Waydroid's graphics into a separate Linux Mint window while keeping the existing Deck desktop session intact.

## Waydroid feasibility audit — Binder result

This is the first significant compatibility finding, and unfortunately it is a serious blocker.

Your Steam Deck kernel reports:  
\# CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_IPC is not set  
CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_IPC\_RUST=y

CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_DEVICES=""

And the device checks found:

* No /dev/binder\*, /dev/anbox-binder\* or /dev/vndbinder\* devices.  
* No Binder or Ashmem modules currently loaded.  
* Your user is deck, UID/GID 1000, with wheel membership. No special Waydroid permissions are currently present.

Important nuance: CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_IPC\_RUST=y means the kernel has the Rust Binder IPC implementation enabled, even though the traditional Binder IPC option is disabled. So we should not conclude that Binder is entirely absent just from the first line. However, the empty CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_DEVICES setting and missing device nodes mean we have not established that Waydroid can access the Binder interfaces it needs.

The graphics check was interrupted by a missing fi in my command card. That was my mistake; it did not modify anything.

## A more precise finding: the kernel has Rust Binder

I checked the exact configuration against the Waydroid project's issue tracker. There is a reported compatibility problem involving the same three kernel settings you have:  
CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_IPC\_RUST=y  
\# CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_IPC is not set

CONFIG\_ANDROID\_BINDER\_DEVICES=""

The report describes Waydroid driver detection and Binder device setup problems on newer Arch-based kernels. It is particularly relevant because your SteamOS kernel is also in the Linux 7.2 family. The issue was closed, but the page still contains a September 2026 report describing a workaround; that is not proof of a clean, officially supported solution.

![]()

GitHub

\+1

So I would revise the assessment:

* Binder support: present in the kernel through the Rust implementation.  
* Binder device access: not currently established; no device nodes were found.  
* Waydroid compatibility: uncertain, with a directly relevant upstream issue.  
* SteamOS changes: not justified by this audit. The workaround described online involves persistent host-level changes, which I would not recommend adopting without much more scrutiny.

This is not yet a definitive rejection, but it is a meaningful warning.

```
for f in /sys/class/drm/card0/device/vendor /sys/class/drm/card0/device/device /sys/class/drm/card0/device/driver; do
  if [ -e "$f" ]; then
    printf '%s: ' "$f"
    readlink -f "$f" 2>/dev/null || cat "$f" 2>/dev/null
  fi
done

echo
echo '=== GRAPHICS UTILITIES ==='
for tool in glxinfo eglinfo vainfo vulkaninfo; do
  command -v "$tool" 2>/dev/null || echo "$tool: not installed"
done
```

Why this check matters: if BinderFS is available, the missing /dev/binder devices may be a device-initialisation issue rather than missing kernel functionality. We can then assess whether Waydroid's current implementation can use it without changing SteamOS.

## Waydroid audit — updated findings

This is a better result than the missing device nodes initially suggested.

Your kernel has the Rust Binder driver and Binder filesystem support:  
nodev binder

rust\_binder: present

That means Binder support is compiled into the running kernel and the Binder filesystem is registered. However:

* BinderFS is not mounted.  
* /dev/binderfs does not exist.  
* No Binder device nodes are currently exposed.

This distinction matters: we have evidence that the kernel can support BinderFS, but we have not yet demonstrated that Waydroid can initialise and use it on SteamOS.

Your graphics driver is also confirmed:

driver: amdgpu

That is the AMD GPU driver used by the Steam Deck. The installed glxinfo, eglinfo and vulkaninfo utilities give us ways to inspect the graphics stack without installing anything.

Current assessment: the kernel has a promising Binder foundation, and the Deck's AMD graphics stack is present. The missing piece is whether the Binder implementation and Waydroid's container setup work together on this SteamOS build.

### Important discovery: SteamOS is close to a working Binder configuration

I found a particularly relevant report from September–October 2026 involving Linux 7.2, AMD graphics and Waydroid.

It describes a system with almost exactly your kernel configuration. The Rust Binder driver can expose Waydroid-compatible devices, but the required device setup depends on the kernel's Binder parameters. The report also identifies a separate Rust Binder stability problem under real Android workloads.

## Waydroid audit — Binder parameter finding

This output confirms another important detail.  
/sys/module/rust\_binder/parameters/rust\_devices

rust\_devices:

The rust\_devices parameter exists, but its value is empty.

Combined with the earlier results:

* Rust Binder is compiled into and active in the kernel.  
* BinderFS is registered.  
* The Rust Binder device list is empty.  
* No Binder devices are exposed.  
* No BinderFS mount exists.  
* Your kernel command line contains no Binder-related parameters.

This suggests the kernel has the necessary Binder infrastructure, but it has not been configured to expose the device interfaces Waydroid needs.

The GPU identification is also conclusive:  
vendor: 0x1002  
device: 0x1435

driver: amdgpu

That is the AMD Van Gogh APU platform used by the Steam Deck. The Deck has the correct general GPU hardware for hardware-accelerated Android graphics, subject to the Waydroid/Mesa integration working correctly.

### One important correction to our interpretation

The empty rust\_devices value does not necessarily mean Waydroid cannot use Binder.

The Linux kernel source shows that this parameter specifies which Binder devices are created automatically when BinderFS is mounted. With an empty value, those default devices are not created. BinderFS can still provide a binder-control interface through which devices can be created dynamically.

![]()

Git at Google

\+1

That gives us two distinct possibilities:

1. Waydroid may be able to create its Binder devices dynamically using BinderFS.  
2. Waydroid's current setup may expect pre-created devices and require additional configuration.

We need to establish which applies to the current Waydroid release before drawing conclusions.

| Android CPU workload on Deck | Architecture supports it |
| Android GPU workload on Deck | Hardware suitable |
| Binder integration | Not yet verified |
| Individual Android windows on Mint | Not yet verified |
| Remote input and display | Not yet verified |

One clarification about your original requirement: Mint will still use some CPU/GPU resources to decode and display the remote video. The Android application itself, its CPU execution, and its GPU rendering can remain on the Deck.

My recommendation: don't create waydroid-box yet. Let's investigate the current upstream Waydroid BinderFS setup and its compatibility with Rust Binder first. That is now the most important unresolved technical question.

No changes have been made to SteamOS.

```
- Do not repeat completed tests without a specific reason.
- No destructive cleanup.
- No image pruning.
- No container deletion outside the disposable test itself.
- No host configuration changes without explicit approval.
- No autostart.
- No package installation on SteamOS during the audit.

2.5 Security philosophy

A technically successful test is not automatically an acceptable
security configuration.

In particular:
- CAP_SYS_ADMIN is powerful.
- Unconfined seccomp is not a proposed production setting.
- A nested namespace is not proof of safe nested LXC isolation.
- Device access is not proof of correct Android Binder operation.
- A working GPU device is not proof of hardware-accelerated Android.

======================================================================
5. WAYDROID ARCHITECTURE EXAMINATION
======================================================================

5.1 Waydroid is not a conventional standalone Android VM

Waydroid uses the host Linux kernel.

It starts an Android environment through an inner LXC container.

The architecture therefore involves nested containerization:

SteamOS
  |
  +-- Rootless Podman / Distrobox
        |
        +-- Waydroid userspace
              |
              +-- Inner LXC Android container
                    |
                    +-- Android services
                    +-- Android applications

This is a major difference from running an ordinary Linux application
inside Podman.

5.2 Binder requirement

Android requires Binder IPC.

Waydroid must provide appropriate Binder devices to its Android
environment.

The relevant devices are:

- binder
- vndbinder
- hwbinder

BinderFS can dynamically create these devices.

5.3 Graphics requirement

Waydroid needs access to suitable graphics devices.

The Android environment must be able to use the Deck's AMD GPU
through the appropriate graphics stack.

The render device must be made available to the inner Android
environment without granting excessive host access.

5.4 LXC requirements

Upstream Waydroid LXC configuration includes broad capabilities
and system integration.

Capabilities and operations encountered in the source examination
include:

- sys_admin
- net_admin
- mknod
- chown
- sys_chroot

The LXC configuration also deals with:

- cgroups
- sysfs
- proc
- device handling
- namespaces
- mount operations

This is a significant obstacle for a rootless nested deployment.

5.5 Waydroid networking

Waydroid's network script configures networking for Android.

The examined behavior includes:

- Creating waydroid0.
- Configuring forwarding.
- Configuring firewall rules.
- Configuring DHCP/DNS-related behavior.
- Configuring NAT.

A particularly important finding:

The network script enables host IP forwarding.

The stop script does not restore the previous ip_forward value.

This is unacceptable as an unexamined side effect in the intended
container-only architecture.

5.6 Desktop integration

Waydroid's graphical session needs access to:

- KDE Wayland compositor.
- Wayland socket.
- XDG_RUNTIME_DIR.
- D-Bus session.
- Audio/Pulse-related session paths.
- Relevant environment variables.

The SSH session does not automatically inherit these.

5.7 ADB

An Android-side ADB connection is not equivalent to exposing ADB
to the LAN.

A local Android ADB endpoint on port 5555 must not be confused with
a LAN-exposed ADB service.

No LAN ADB exposure is intended.

======================================================================
11. CURRENT RESULTS — WHAT HAS ACTUALLY BEEN PROVEN
======================================================================

PROVEN:

1. SteamOS has the required Rust Binder kernel implementation.

2. BinderFS is available.

3. BinderFS can be mounted inside a disposable rootless Podman
   container when CAP_SYS_ADMIN is granted.

4. BinderFS devices can be created inside that container.

5. The Binder device can be opened.

6. BINDER_VERSION responds successfully.

7. The reported Binder protocol version is 8.

8. The host can create nested user namespaces.

9. A rootless Podman container can create a nested user namespace.

10. The nested UID/GID mapping can succeed with the capability
    combination:

    SETUID + SETGID + SETFCAP

11. SETPCAP can be omitted from that successful test.

12. Rootless Podman networking and DNS work.

13. Disposable namespace-local network operations work.

14. Host IP forwarding remains disabled during the audit.

NOT PROVEN:

1. Actual Waydroid startup inside Podman.

2. Actual nested LXC startup.

3. Binder transactions.

4. Android Binder service communication.

5. Binder device delegation into inner LXC.

6. LXC cgroup operation under the available cgroup delegation.

7. Android GPU acceleration.

8. Android access to the AMD render device through nested LXC.

9. Wayland graphical integration.

10. Audio integration.

11. Remote display streaming to Linux Mint.

12. Remote keyboard/mouse input.

13. Waydroid networking without host-side changes.

14. Safe long-term operation under a restricted capability set.

======================================================================
12. CURRENT BLOCKERS AND RISKS
======================================================================

12.1 Nested LXC privileges

The successful user namespace test is encouraging, but LXC may
require more than user namespace creation.

The following remain to be investigated:

- Mount operations.
- Cgroup operations.
- Device creation and access.
- Namespace setup.
- Capability transitions.
- LXC security profiles.
- Seccomp compatibility.

12.2 CAP_SYS_ADMIN

BinderFS mounting required CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the disposable
container test.

This capability is broad.

We must not assume that granting it permanently to the proposed
Waydroid container is acceptable.

The test proves that BinderFS mounting is possible under that
configuration, not that the resulting production security posture
is acceptable.

12.3 Cgroup delegation

Host cgroup v2 controllers observed:

cpuset cpu io memory hugetlb pids rdma misc dmem

Host subtree control included:

cpu memory pids dmem

Inside the restricted rootless container:

- /sys/fs/cgroup is read-only.
- Visible controllers were cpu, memory and pids.
- subtree_control was empty.

This indicates restricted cgroup delegation.

A nested LXC configuration may be unable to manage the cgroups
it expects.

This is a significant unresolved obstacle.

12.4 Waydroid networking

Waydroid networking scripts can modify host forwarding and
firewall/NAT state.

The original architecture is not acceptable unless those side
effects can be contained or avoided.

12.5 Graphics

The Deck has AMD Van Gogh graphics and working host graphics.

That does not establish that Android can use the GPU from inside
nested LXC.

12.6 Remote interface

The initial goal is not merely to run Android on the Deck.

The Android screen must be available on the Linux Mint PC.

This requires a separate remote graphics/input solution.

SSH alone is insufficient.

======================================================================
13. NEXT TESTS — PROPOSED ORDER
======================================================================

The next tests should be selected based on the evidence already
collected.

Do not repeat BinderFS or basic host namespace tests.

PRIORITY 1 — Test 20 security profile comparison

Test 20 passed with:

SETUID
SETGID
SETFCAP

Seccomp:
unconfined

NoNewPrivs:
0

The next important question is whether the same three-capability
combination works with Podman's default seccomp profile.

This is important because unconfined seccomp should not become
the assumed production configuration.

Test:
Same capability set, default seccomp, otherwise identical.

Possible outcomes:

- PASS: nested mapping works with default seccomp.
- FAIL: seccomp interaction remains an obstacle.

PRIORITY 2 — Verify exact UID/GID mapping behavior

Investigate why SETFCAP changes the mapping result.

Do not claim a universal kernel requirement without further
evidence.

PRIORITY 3 — LXC feasibility

Only after the namespace/security profile is understood.

Use a disposable container and a minimal LXC test environment.

Do not install Waydroid yet.

The objective is to determine whether LXC can create and manage
its inner container under the intended rootless restrictions.

PRIORITY 4 — Cgroup behavior

Determine whether LXC can operate with the available cgroup
delegation or whether the required operations are blocked.

Do not modify host cgroup settings.

PRIORITY 5 — Binder device delegation

Determine whether Binder devices created in the outer container
can be made available to the inner LXC environment safely.

Do not assume that successful BinderFS creation proves this.

PRIORITY 6 — GPU device access

Test the AMD render node with the minimum required device access.

No broad /dev passthrough.

PRIORITY 7 — Wayland/audio integration

Only after the Android runtime and graphics requirements are
understood.

Use the existing desktop session.

PRIORITY 8 — Networking

Investigate a container-contained networking model.

Host IP forwarding must not be changed as a side effect.

PRIORITY 9 — Remote display/input

Determine how the Android window can be displayed and controlled
from Linux Mint while computation remains on the Deck.

======================================================================
14. AUDIT DECISION CRITERIA
======================================================================

The project may proceed only if the following can be demonstrated:

A. Container isolation

Waydroid runs inside rootless Podman/Distrobox.

B. Nested LXC

The inner Android container can start without privileged mode
or unacceptable host capabilities.

C. Binder

Android can use Binder correctly through the container boundary.

D. GPU

Android can use the Deck GPU with appropriate restricted device
access.

E. Cgroups

LXC can operate with available cgroup delegation.

F. Networking

Waydroid networking does not require uncontrolled host changes.

G. Desktop integration

Waydroid can use the existing Deck Wayland session.

H. Remote interface

The Android interface can be displayed and controlled from
Linux Mint.

I. Lifecycle

Start/stop remains manual.

No boot autostart.

J. Recovery

The project can be recreated after a SteamOS reset without
requiring broad host modifications.

If any mandatory criterion cannot be met securely, the correct
decision is NO-GO under the current architecture.

======================================================================
15. FINAL ASSESSMENT AT REVISION 2.0
======================================================================

STATUS:

PARTIAL FEASIBILITY DEMONSTRATED.

The audit has passed several important low-level checkpoints:

- Rootless Podman baseline.
- Rootless networking and DNS.
- Host BinderFS.
- BinderFS inside rootless Podman with CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
- Binder device creation.
- Binder device opening.
- Binder protocol query.
- Nested user namespace creation.
- Nested UID/GID mapping with SETUID, SETGID and SETFCAP.

The nested namespace investigation has materially improved the
feasibility picture.

The smallest successful capability combination tested so far is:

CAP_SETUID
CAP_SETGID
CAP_SETFCAP

However, the successful mapping test used:

seccomp=unconfined
NoNewPrivs=0

The next security comparison is therefore important.

The largest remaining technical risks are:

1. Actual nested LXC operation.
2. Cgroup delegation.
3. Binder device use by Android.
4. GPU access through nested LXC.
5. Waydroid networking.
6. Wayland/audio integration.
7. Remote Android display and input.

No Waydroid installation has been performed.

No existing project has been modified.

No native SteamOS Waydroid installation is permitted.

No host IP forwarding change has been made.

The project remains in the feasibility audit phase.
```
